claims.text: The Herald Tribune series of November 1955 lists 'Bell Aircraft of Buffalo, builders of the first piloted airplane to fly faster than sound and a current jet vertical take-off and landing airplane' among the aircraft industry firms 'now participating or actively interested in gravity'.

claims.source: Ansel E. Talbert, 'New Air Dream, Planes Flying Outside Gravity', New York Herald Tribune, 22 November 1955, p. 1. https://archive.org/download/talbert3ny/talbert3ny_djvu.txt
claims.text: Lawrence D. Bell told Talbert: 'Aviation as we know it is on the threshold of amazing new concepts', and 'The Wright Brothers proved that man does not have to be earth-bound. Our next step will be to prove that we can operate outside the earth's atmosphere and the third will be to operate outside the gravity of the earth.'

claims.source: Talbert, New York Herald Tribune, 22 November 1955, p. 1 and caption. https://archive.org/download/talbert3ny/talbert3ny_djvu.txt
claims.text: The same article reports that Bell's company had in the preceding days made the first powered flights with its new Bell X-2 rocket plane, and that it was testing a jet vertical-rising-and-landing aircraft. Its photograph caption names three Air Force test pilots with Bell: Lt. Col. Frank J. Everest, Maj. Charles Yeager and Maj. Arthur Murray.

The opened articles are dated November 1955, and the words attributed to Bell in them do not use the term electrogravitics.

desc: Bell Aircraft Corporation of Buffalo, New York is one of the aircraft firms named in Ansel Talbert's November 1955 New York Herald Tribune series as participating or actively interested in gravity research, and its founder and president Lawrence D. Bell is quoted in the series directly. It reaches this board through the Danny Jones corpus, where a guest names it alongside Martin as a company making public electrogravitics claims in 1953. The opened press record puts the claims two years later and puts them in more careful language than the transcript does: Bell speaks of operating outside the earth's gravity as a third step after atmospheric flight, not of a working engine.
